problem_statement: The CoAP message parser is run on a message held in a buffer, with a known byte placed immediately after that message. After the run, the byte following the message has a different value than it had before, even though it is outside the data that was handed to the parser. This is observed when the message's payload reaches the end of the receive buffer — a single datagram that fills the buffer, reachable with a payload of 64 or fewer bytes, is enough to reach it — when the payload is longer than the largest allowed chunk and is truncated, leaving a byte that still belongs to the message changed, and when the payload is binary data that itself contains null bytes. In each of these cases the byte immediately after the received payload is the one that is found to have changed. The expected behavior is that running the parser leaves every byte outside the received data unchanged, and that the payload it reports — its length and its contents — matches the input exactly, so that an adjacent byte and a following byte are both preserved.

superseded_statements.problem_statement: coap_parse_message() overwrites the byte immediately after the received payload with a null terminator, writing one byte past the message that the transport supplied; RFC 7252 delimits the payload by datagram length and never requires a terminator. The observe-client example also used %*s (a field width) where %.*s (a precision) was intended, which only worked because of the spurious terminator.
check_issues: `problem_statement` gives the fix away: "coap_parse_message() overwrites the byte immediately after the received payload with a null terminator, writing one byte past the message that the transport supplied"; "RFC 7252 delimits the payload by datagram length and never requires a terminator"; "The observe-client example also used %*s (a field width) where %.*s (a precision) was intended, which only worked because of the spurious terminator". Describe only the observable symptom, its trigger and the required behavior, not what the code checks or must do internally

causal_chain: The upstream native test builds each CoAP message in a buffer that places a known canary byte directly after the message, runs the parser on it, and then inspects the canary and the reported payload. The keeps-canary case builds a 10-byte payload and asserts that the parse succeeds, that the reported length and contents are correct, and that the canary after the message is unchanged; in the unfixed code the canary is found changed. The oversized case builds a payload longer than the maximum chunk size, records the byte that follows the truncation point (which still belongs to the message), and asserts that byte is unchanged; in the unfixed code it is found changed. The null-bytes case builds a 4-byte payload containing null bytes and asserts its length and contents are intact and the canary is unchanged; in the unfixed code the canary is found changed. These three assertions fail before the production fix. The empty-payload case checks that a payload marker with no following byte is rejected, which is independent of this behavior and passes both before and after.
